title: The STRONG Method
coreMove: Organize pitch control into the STRONG sequence and see how each move sets up the next.
sourcePressure: Bridge chapter: the first two problem chapters become a controllable six-step operating sequence rather than a diagnosis with no method.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: The writer must avoid making STRONG a flat mnemonic summary; the point is sequence dependence after the audience-filter problem.

hook: Six steps can fix every pitch
counterintuition: A framework is not a script
tryThisNow: Rate your pitch on six steps

exampleSpecs.domain: offshore wind developer preparing a port-authority lease pitch
exampleSpecs.audience: a project lead with engineering, finance, and political risk all competing for airtime
exampleSpecs.stakes: the lease vote stalls if the pitch opens with turbines before control of the room is set
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she rearranges six index cards on the ferry terminal bench until frame comes before megawatt output and decision comes last
exampleSpecs.firstImage: six colored index cards weighted by a ferry token

exampleSpecs.domain: minor-league baseball sponsorship director selling a naming package to a regional bank
exampleSpecs.audience: a sponsorship director who usually starts with attendance numbers
exampleSpecs.stakes: the bank treats the offer as logo inventory unless the sequence builds status and desire first
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he crosses out the old attendance-first order and places the community-story card before the premium-access card
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a stadium seating chart folded beside a stack of sponsor lanyards

exampleSpecs.domain: telemedicine compliance lead pitching a remote-triage rollout to emergency physicians
exampleSpecs.audience: a clinician-administrator who must win a room that distrusts workflow tools
exampleSpecs.stakes: the rollout dies if physicians hear software before status and patient-flow stakes
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: after a failed pilot meeting, she labels where she skipped intrigue and jumped from story straight to decision
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a printed pilot agenda with two coffee rings and red checkmarks

exampleSpecs.domain: boutique hotel owner seeking a construction loan for a fire-damaged inn
exampleSpecs.audience: an owner whose emotional story needs order to become financeable
exampleSpecs.stakes: the lender hears sentimental restoration instead of controlled demand and repayment logic
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: he lays loan documents in sequence and notices the hookpoint only works after the occupancy rebound story
exampleSpecs.firstImage: charred porch baluster beside a clean loan term sheet

exampleSpecs.domain: ocean-cleanup robotics team pitching a marina pilot to harbor commissioners
exampleSpecs.audience: engineers who tend to demo the machine before defining the room's frame
exampleSpecs.stakes: commissioners dismiss the robot as a gadget before seeing the debris cost
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the team lead shuts the demo case and starts instead with who controls the marina's reputation after holiday trash weekends
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sealed robot case beside a bucket of tangled fishing line

exampleSpecs.domain: university licensing officer pitching a battery patent to a materials manufacturer
exampleSpecs.audience: a licensing officer who has the data but no live sequence
exampleSpecs.stakes: the manufacturer files the patent as speculative unless intrigue and prize build before terms
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she asks the room to imagine the competitor signing first, then moves the terms sheet to the end of the packet
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a patent diagram clipped to a graphite sample pouch

skillTargets: order STRONG moves in live scenarios
explain why one stage cannot carry the whole pitch
evaluate sequence changes without turning them into rigid scripts

tryThisNowSpec: Write the six STRONG moves as six one-line beats for your current pitch, then put a slash where you usually rush or skip.
